deep.reconstruction:
PART A: conclusion of the comparison argument for highly composite numbers, continued from f.54.

Setting on f.54. N = exp(θ(p_1)+θ(p_2)+...) is highly composite. Here p_r is the largest prime whose exponent in N is at least r. Hence d(N) = 2^{π(p_1)} (3/2)^{π(p_2)} (4/3)^{π(p_3)} ...

The competitor is N' = N·exp(θ(q_r)+θ(q_s)−θ(p_r)−θ(p_s)), with q_r > p_r, q_s < p_s and
- π(q_r) = π(p_r)+n,
- π(p_s)−π(q_s) = [n log(1+1/r)/log(1+1/s)].

Then d(N') ≥ d(N). Since N is highly composite, N' ≥ N, i.e. θ(q_r)−θ(p_r) ≥ θ(p_s)−θ(q_s).

f.54 ends with the elementary bound: for α > β, (π(α)−π(β)) log β ≤ θ(α)−θ(β) ≤ (π(α)−π(β)) log α.

This page:
1. Apply the upper bound to the left side (α = q_r, β = p_r) and the lower bound to the right side (α = p_s, β = q_s). This gives {π(q_r)−π(p_r)} log q_r ≥ θ(q_r)−θ(p_r) ≥ θ(p_s)−θ(q_s) ≥ {π(p_s)−π(q_s)} log q_s.
2. Substitute (1) from f.54: n log q_r ≥ [n log(1+1/r)/log(1+1/s)] log q_s.
3. He then notes that q_r and q_s must be expressed through p_r and p_s, e.g. via π(q_r) = π(p_r)+n and the prime number theorem. The argument is not continued on this page.

The aim is to show that, roughly, log p_r / log p_s ≈ log(1+1/r)/log(1+1/s). This is the familiar result that p_r ≈ p_1^{log(1+1/r)/log 2} for highly composite numbers.

PART B: a separate, unrelated q-series identity.

Definition: f(x,y) = Σ_{k∈Z} x^{k^2} y^k = 1 + x(y+1/y) + x^4(y^2+1/y^2) + ...
Note this is not his usual f(a,b). In terms of the standard f_R(A,B) = Σ A^{k(k+1)/2} B^{k(k−1)/2} = (−A;AB)_∞(−B;AB)_∞(AB;AB)_∞, write q = ab. Then:
- f(√(ab), n√(b/a)) = Σ n^k a^{k(k−1)/2} b^{k(k+1)/2} = f_R(nb, a/n) = (−nb;q)(−a/n;q)(q;q).
- f(√(ab), n√(ab)) = Σ n^k q^{k(k+1)/2} = f_R(nq, 1/n) = (−nq;q)(−1/n;q)(q;q).

Claimed identity: f(√(ab), n√(b/a)) (q;q)_∞^3 / [n f(·,·) f(√(ab), n√(ab))] = 1/(1+n) + Σ_{k≥1} [a^k/(n+q^k) + b^k/(1+n q^k)], with the middle factor f(·,·) as discussed below.

Right side (my rewriting). The k = −m term of a^k/(n+q^k) equals b^m/(1+nq^m). So the right side is the bilateral Lambert series Σ_{k∈Z} a^k/(n+q^k) = (1/n) Σ_k x^k/(1−y q^k), with x = a and y = −1/n. This converges for |ab| < |a| < 1, i.e. |a| < 1 and |b| < 1.

By Kronecker's identity (equivalently the 1ψ1 sum), Σ_k x^k/(1−yq^k) = (q)^2 (xy)(q/(xy)) / [(x)(q/x)(y)(q/y)]. Hence the right side equals (q;q)^2 (−a/n;q)(−nb;q) / [n (a;q)(b;q)(−1/n;q)(−nq;q)].

Comparing with the product forms above, the identity holds exactly when the middle denominator factor is (q;q)(a;q)(b;q) = f_R(−a,−b). In his notation that is f(√(ab), −√(b/a)), equivalently f(−√(ab), √(b/a)). With this reading the identity is a direct consequence of the Jacobi triple product and Kronecker's / Ramanujan's 1ψ1 identity.
errors: Part B: the factor written f(−√(ab), −√(b/a)) cannot be right under his own definition. Since (−1)^{k^2+k} = 1, f(−x,−y) = f(x,y), so as written it equals f_R(a,b) = (−a;q)(−b;q)(q;q).
Sanity check of that slip: at n = 1 the written left side cancels to (q;q)^3/f_R(q,1), which is independent of a, while the right side Σ a^k/(1+q^k) depends on a.
Correct factor: f(√(ab), −√(b/a)) (one minus sign only) = f_R(−a,−b) = (a;q)(b;q)(q;q). This is presumably a slip of the pen.
Part B: no convergence condition is stated; |a| < 1 and |b| < 1 are needed.
Part A: both steps are correct. The θ–π bounds are applied in the right directions: the upper bound on [p_r, q_r] and the lower bound on [q_s, p_s]. The floor bracket is carried over correctly.
Part A: the page stops before the asymptotic step of expressing q_r and q_s via p_r and p_s, so it is incomplete rather than wrong.

results.what: Comparison inequality n log q_r ≥ [n log(1+1/r)/log(1+1/s)] log q_s, obtained by perturbing a highly composite N = exp(Σθ(p_r)). It leads to log p_r/log p_s ≈ log(1+1/r)/log(1+1/s).
results.modern_name: Structure of the exponents of highly composite numbers (p_r ≈ p_1^{log(1+1/r)/log 2})
results.usually_credited_to: Ramanujan, 'Highly composite numbers' (Proc. LMS 1915) and its unpublished continuation (ed. Nicolas–Robin 1997)

results.what: Bilateral Lambert series Σ_{k∈Z} a^k/(n+(ab)^k) expressed as a quotient of theta functions. In his notation: f(√ab, n√(b/a))(q;q)^3/[n f(√ab, −√(b/a)) f(√ab, n√ab)], with q = ab.
results.modern_name: Kronecker's identity / special case of Ramanujan's 1ψ1 summation, combined with the Jacobi triple product
results.usually_credited_to: Kronecker (1881); Ramanujan's 1ψ1 summation (notebooks, made known by Hardy 1940)

deep.surprise_reason: Part A is a draft step from Ramanujan's known highly composite numbers work. Part B is a disguised form of Kronecker's identity, an immediate corollary of Ramanujan's well-known 1ψ1 summation; such identities pervade his notebooks and lost notebook. The unusual theta normalisation f(x,y) = Σ x^{k^2} y^k is a minor curiosity.
